catalog_quote: Prominence In marked difference to European languages, perceptual difference between stressed and unstressed syllables is reportedly not so easy to establish in the languages of South Asia, and Assamese is no exception. Owing to this difficulty, there are also differing views on stress placement rules in Assamese. Notable views on this aspect are those of Kakati (1962), who accepts Grierson's (1895) description, where Assamese is said to follow the pan-Indian system of accenting the heavy penultimate syllable. Goswami (1966) differs from this view and opines that primary stress in Assamese is on the first or second syllable and never moves beyond the second syllable. Some acoustic correlates supporting this view, like low-rise in pitch and longer syllable duration were shown in Mahanta (2001). sweep_summary: Only one work surfaced (twice, under two Glottolog ids): the Goswami & Tamuli 2003 'Asamiya' chapter in Cardona & Jain, The Indo-Aryan Languages (pp. 391-443; chapter DOI 10.4324/9780203945315-10 — Crossref's '-19' DOI for it is wrong). No open full text exists (not on archive.org, HathiTrust or Open Library; T&F paywalled, abstract only; Google Books has no preview), but overlapping Google Books snippet searches reconstruct its entire §9 'Word Stress' paragraph (p. 409) and the dialect stress note (p. 404): primary vs. weak stress, non-contrastive in degree; 'the position of the primary stress is either the first or the second syllable'; Eastern/Central 'medial stress' vs. Western 'strong initial stress', with the medial stress 'optionally being shifted either to the first or the second syllable from the left, and never beyond'. This confirms the catalog's left-edge two-syllable window but is silent on the weight condition and adds dialect variation, so it refines rather than changes the QS-HEDGED coding; Mahanta 2012/2001 remain the deciding sources (and Mahanta 2007 LOT pp. 172-173 and Twaha 2017 §2.5, both on file and read, restate the same weight rule). Saved:, goswami_tamuli2003_gbooks/ (raw fetches),. Acquiring the printed chapter is medium priority (would supply any examples and the full dialect passage). fetches went through direct URLs and the r.jina.ai reader.

new_statements.quote: There are two word stresses: (i) Primary stress /'/, and (ii) Weak stress, phonemically unmarked. There is contrast in position rather than degree of stress in a word as both the stresses do not occur in the same environment. The position of the primary stress is either the first or the second syllable. [p. 404:] Eastern and Central Asamiya have medial stress, whereas Western Asamiya has a strong initial stress. Owing to the influence of Western Asamiya dialect in recent times, the medial stress is optionally being shifted either to the first or the second syllable from the left, and never beyond.

new_statements.reading: Independent reference-grammar statement (Goswami is the senior Assamese phonologist whose 1966/1982 view Mahanta 2012 cites) that primary stress is confined to a left-edge two-syllable window (first or second syllable, 'never beyond') and is not contrastive in degree. It confirms the catalog's window and left edge but gives no weight condition (nothing about closed vs. open syllables) and no default, so it cannot decide QS vs. fixed on its own; the dialect note attributes 'medial stress' to Eastern/Central Asamiya (the standard's base) versus 'strong initial stress' in Western Asamiya, which is a hedge the catalog's tone/notes could carry. The catalog's deciding source (Mahanta 2012 with Mahanta 2001) is more explicit (initial default; sigma2 iff sigma1 light and sigma2 heavy) and stays the deciding source; Goswami & Tamuli is corroboration of the window only. Also re-read in this sweep, fully on file: Mahanta 2007 (LOT 173) pp. 172-173: 'Within the Assamese word stress system, main stress is always assigned to the initial syllable... The second syllable is prominent if it is heavy and the first syllable is light. Otherwise the first syllable is prominent... Heavy syllables never occur as primary stress bearing units beyond the second syllable' — restates the catalog rule verbatim (same author lineage), and Twaha 2017 (IITG thesis) §2.5 p. 2-27 says the same for both SCA and the Nalbari variety.

(2) Deciding source is a 2012 JIPA Illustration by the language's main prosody specialist, resting on her held 2001 metrical/acoustic dissertation; Glottolog's grammar list (CIIL course 1980, dialect monographs, Kakati 1973, Goswami & Tamuli 2003) offers nothing that supersedes it for stress, and CrossRef/IITG-repository searches turned up no independent instrumental study of SCA word-stress placement. sources.quote: 9 WORD STRESS There are two word stresses: (i) Primary stress /'/, and (ii) Weak stress, phonemically unmarked. There is contrast in position rather than degree of stress in a word as both the stresses do not occur in the same environment. The position of the primary stress is either the first or the second syllable. There are two stresses at the utterance level: (i) Sentence stress /'/, and (ii) Emphatic stress /"/. Phonetically there seems to be no difference between the emphatic and sentence stress.
